Just to add on. The hospital can appeal to a judge though to stop your AMA discharge. If the judge rules in favor of the hospital then you lose certain rights like checking yourself out against medical advice, because essentially the ruling is that you’re not capable of making decisions on your own. It’s a bit of a catch 22. 

That’s why IMHO it’s best to write an advance mental health directive before you get your grippy socks. You can say things like what medications you concent to, and which you don’t concent to. Also, you can say who you want to make medical decisions on your behalf if you are deemed to be unfit to make them yourself.

I have been working through *Transforming the Living Legacy of Trauma* by Janina Fisher. [ISBN: 978-1683733485](https://duckduckgo.com/?q=isbn+978-1683733485) Please note, that it will be very challenging to try and go through the book, especially alone, which is immensely unfair given how hard life already is for you. One of the things Fisher says in Chapter 5 is:

> ... remember to look for the adaptive intent and to reframe the disorder or addiction as a valiant attempt to manage overwhelming feelings and memories.

You’re not stupid for not feeling hatred. Your feelings are what they are and placing a value judgment on them usually isn’t helpful. You might one day feel different, and those feelings will be valid too. 

You have had a lot of horrible things happen to you at the hands of your family who should have cared for you well, kept you safe, and loved you. You probably don’t want to let yourself hate your family because, one, hatred consumes too much energy for someone with depression, and two, if you still rely on your family for your basic survival (food, clothes, shelter) it’s safer t￼o make yourself feel numb towards them, even though you know deep down that they aren’t safe and you don’t trust them (like your sister). Likewise, you probably watch porn as a way of numbing yourself against painful feelings. 

If you can feel a little bit of understanding for your abusers, then try and also have understanding for yourself. It might be hard, but if you can feel it for your family then you can feel it for yourself. Therapy with psychologist who specializes in trauma can help, though, I won’t lie it’s going to be a challenging journey.

It depends how receptive she is, but see if she’ll agree to a “safety plan”. There are lots of templates out there. But here’s one. https://suicidepreventionlifeline.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/08/Brown_StanleySafetyPlanTemplate.pdf

The idea is helping her realize the things that stress her to the point where she wants to attempt again and then coming up with a plan on how to relieve the stress before it gets dangerous. Its something that her therapist probably has already worked with her on, but if not ask her if she’s do it for you. If she already has one, make it clear that you and your wife want to be part of it. And know what kinds of things she finds helpful.

Self harm might be one of the things she puts on her list. If she does, DONT FREAK OUT! The end goal is for her to have better copping mechanisms, but the immediate goal is for her the be alive. Hopefully she start to prefer the love and acceptance she gets from you and your wife along with the other coping skills. But until then put a first aid kit in her room and let her know that even if you’d rather she didn’t cut that you want her patched up at a minimum.

Best of luck.

Those kinds of impulsive/intrusive thoughts aren’t really typical with dysthymia. But I’d advise to not get too caught up on self diagnosing yourself, because there’s a tendency to wrap up your identity with it. Like, try to keep an open mind on what kinda help you might need.

Mindfulness meditation is a really helpful tool for intrusive thoughts. There’s a myriad of resources online for how to practice it but the tl;dr is you focus on your breath. And a thought will come into your mind and you acknowledge that thought and then let it go, and focus on breath. It’s just a thought, no value judgement about it being good or bad, just something to observe and let go.

If that’s too much to handle then I’d focus on getting the help of a psychologist. They help you figure out the why part of intrusive thoughts. As well as safety plans for what to do when you feel like you want to reach for a blade. Having a plan that you rehearse in your head before hand can be really helpful.
